html:
A long Latin poem by Lucretius, written in the first century BCE, that explains the philosophy of Epicurus to Romans. Its six books run to about 7,400 lines.

Its message is that there is nothing to fear. Everything, including the soul, is made of tiny atoms moving through empty space. The gods exist but take no part in the world, so they do not punish anyone. The soul dies with the body, so death is nothing to us. Lucretius describes how worlds form and fall apart, how life and human society began, and ends with a grim picture of the plague of Athens.

Cicero mentions the poem in a letter of 54 BCE, praising its skill. Lucretius himself is almost unknown.

The poem nearly vanished. In 1417 the Italian book hunter Poggio Bracciolini found a copy in a German monastery. It spread Epicurean and atomist ideas through the Renaissance and helped prepare the ground for modern science.
